Programming the car is a volition formed in advance about who will die, so the makers own that intention whatever the rule, and impartial compassion counts the passenger as neither more nor less than anyone else. Intention weighs as much as outcome. A rule chosen to reduce suffering, honestly published, is made from a different volition than one chosen to protect sales by favouring the buyer, even if both sometimes kill the same people.

There is no fixed, bounded self that makes the passenger's suffering more real than a pedestrian's. Later traditions argue from this to impartial compassion, which weighs each being's suffering alike, and that points to the rule that causes the least. A carmaker publishes its rule, explains that it gives every life equal weight, and reviews every fatal crash to see whether the rule did what it was meant to.

A Confucian will object that the maker has taken responsibility for the passenger in particular, and impartial compassion that ignores this relationship treats a betrayal of trust as fairness. Compassion does not ignore the passenger's trust; it refuses to let that trust cost others their lives. The honest course is to tell passengers the rule before they ride, so that no one is betrayed and no life is counted twice. That is why the Buddhist Ethicist asks not only what the system was built to do but whom it is hurting now.

I accept the motion. The compassion later traditions draw from there being no fixed, separate self has no ground for counting the passenger's life above the lives in the road. Non-harm covers what one incites as well as what one does. A rule written into a car is an intention to cause a death in certain circumstances, so the question is not whether the makers will cause deaths but which deaths they will intend, and fewer is better.

The rule's effects arise from many conditions, including how the roads are built and who walks them. The makers must keep examining what the rule does once it is on the road, because a rule that minimises deaths in tests may do otherwise among real people. An engineer who writes the crash rule asks herself each week whether she would accept it as a pedestrian, as a passenger, and as the parent of either.

We should focus on making them safe instead of worrying about rare dilemmas that are mostly in philosophy classes. Two lives are more than one, that is just maths. I do not see why this is even a question. The car should save as many people as it can and that is the end of it.
